title: Quadratic Equations
tagline: Year 2 — Factorisation, the formula, roots and their relations

introduction.overview: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0. It can have two, one or no real solutions (roots). The methods are factorisation, completing the square and the quadratic formula. Three relations about the roots (sum, product, and the discriminant) answer many aptitude questions without solving the equation at all.
introduction.placementRelevance: Quadratic equations are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds, both as a direct "find the roots" item and as a word problem (rectangle area, consecutive integers, price and quantity).
introduction.realWorldContext: Projectile motion, areas and breakeven calculations often lead to quadratic equations.

learningObjectives: Solve quadratics by factorisation and the formula
Use the sum and product of roots
Use the discriminant to decide the nature of roots
Form a quadratic from given roots
Solve word problems that lead to quadratics

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: x² + px + q = (x + m)(x + n) when m + n = p and mn = q. The square of a real number is never negative.

coreDefinitions: Quadratic equation: ax² + bx + c = 0, a ≠ 0. Roots: values of x that satisfy it.
Discriminant: D = b² − 4ac. D > 0: two real roots; D = 0: equal roots; D < 0: no real roots.
Sum of roots = −b/a. Product of roots = c/a.
Equation with roots α and β: x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The graph of a quadratic is a parabola. The roots are where it crosses the x-axis. The discriminant tells whether it crosses twice, touches once, or misses the axis.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: First try factorisation: look for two numbers with the right sum and product. If that fails, use the formula or the discriminant.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Factorisation
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: x² + px + q = (x + m)(x + n), m + n = p, mn = q

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Symmetric expressions
importantRulesAndFormulas.whenToUse: Values of expressions in the roots.

mainNarrative: Factorise when you can. x² − 5x + 6 needs two numbers with sum −5 and product 6: −2 and −3, so (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0 and x = 2 or x = 3. For x² − 9, use the difference of squares: x = ±3.
The quadratic formula handles every case. For x² − 6x + 4 = 0, D = 36 − 16 = 20, so x = (6 ± √20)/2 = 3 ± √5. The discriminant tells you before solving: D = b² − 4ac.
For 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0, D = 16 − 24 = −8 < 0, so there are no real roots. When D = 0, the two roots are equal, as in x² − 4x + 4 = (x − 2)².

Use the sum and product of roots to avoid solving. If α and β are the roots of x² − 5x + 6 = 0, then α + β = 5 and αβ = 6, so α² + β² = 25 − 12 = 13. To form an equation with roots 2 and 5, write x² − 7x + 10 = 0.

Word problems: let the unknown be x and form the equation. The product of two consecutive positive integers is 132: x(x + 1) = 132, so x² + x − 132 = 0 and x = 11. For a rectangle of area 48 whose length is 2 more than its breadth: b(b + 2) = 48, so b = 6.

deepDiveAspects.title: Rejecting roots
deepDiveAspects.content: In word problems, a negative root may not make sense (negative length or age). Check each root against the context.

deepDiveAspects.title: Biquadratic type
deepDiveAspects.content: An equation like x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0 is quadratic in x². Put y = x²: y² − 5y + 4 = 0 gives y = 1 or 4, so x = ±1, ±2: four real roots.

solvedExamples.title: Factorisation
solvedExamples.question: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: Find numbers with sum −5 and product 6.

solvedExamples.title: Symmetric expression
solvedExamples.question: If α and β are the roots of x² − 5x + 6 = 0, find α² + β².

solvedExamples.title: Word problem
solvedExamples.question: The product of two consecutive positive integers is 132. Find the smaller integer.

shortcutMethods.title: Sum-product shortcuts

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Read sum and product from the coefficients; use D to decide the nature of roots; form the equation from roots directly.

rulesForApplication: Reject roots that do not fit the story.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Test options by substituting into the equation.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Often the answer is an integer, so factorisation works.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I find the nature of roots?
Can I form an equation with roots 2 and 5?
